characters: Anum: a lively seven-year-old Ghanaian girl with two neat puff hairstyles with yellow beads, wearing a bright sky-blue patterned dress.
Uncle Ocloo: her kind adult uncle with a warm smile in a rolled-sleeve indigo work shirt and brown trousers, who mends bicycles.
Her little brother: a five-year-old Ghanaian boy in an orange T-shirt and shorts holding a colourful diamond paper kite.

narrationPlan.voice: A lively girl’s voice for Anum; a warm uncle’s voice for Uncle Ocloo
narrationPlan.pace: Light and playful, with a breath before each trick (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A breezy tune with soft whooshing sounds (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Bicycle repair shops and kites are common sights in Ghanaian communities. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on the properties and uses of air (B2.2.1.4.2, B3.2.1.4.2).
The balloon activity is safe with adult help. Children must not put a balloon in their mouth or chew it, and broken pieces are thrown away at once.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the claim that air takes up space and has many uses against NaCCA B2.2.1.4.2 and B3.2.1.4.2.
Check the safety note on balloons (young children can choke on balloon pieces).

teacherGuide.overview: A balloon, a paper fan and a bicycle pump show that air is real even though we cannot see it. Children learn that air takes up space and has many uses. Based on NaCCA Science standards on air.
learningGoals: Say that air takes up space.
Say that moving air is wind.
beforeReading: Ask: can you see air? How do you know it is there?
whileReading: Let children wave a paper fan and say what they feel.
afterReading: Blow up a balloon with the teacher and talk about what filled it.
Make a poster of five uses of air.
discussion: Why does a tyre go flat when air escapes?
What would happen if there were no air?
reflection: Where did you feel air today?

support: Use a paper fan and a feather to feel and see moving air.
stretch: Test whether a kite flies better on a windy day or a still day.

culturalNotes: Bicycle repair shops and kites are common sights in Ghanaian communities. The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on the properties and uses of air (B2.2.1.4.2, B3.2.1.4.2).
The balloon activity is safe with adult help. Children must not put a balloon in their mouth or chew it, and broken pieces are thrown away at once.
localiseThis: Use a bicycle, motorbike or football pump from your own area.
Keep balloons away from small children’s mouths.
